## 3. Rung C and the repair's bodies (item 2)

Each variant was taken out in the shadow. All runs are instrumented and idle.

| run | stage | apis | component | table |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| I5: repair in | 935 s | 293.8 s | 620.1 s | 39 / 38 / none |
| I4: rung C out | 826 s | 251.6 s | 554.3 s | 40 / 39, plus `:2623`, row 686's site, which rung C repaired |
| I6: repair out | 668 s | 298.5 s | 331 s, then the crash | 1 / 0, the crash at `:3059` |
| I7: the fix | 339 s | 68.0 s | 263.0 s | equal to I5 |
| I8: the fix, rung C out | 274 s | 60.9 s | 205.0 s | equal to I4 |
| I9: the JVM switch, no fix | 652 s | 92.0 s | 528.9 s | equal to I5 |

**The repair: +267 s.** In order of checking, the component has 229 declarations before Array3:

| run | the 229 before Array3 | Array3 | the 257 after Array3 |
|---|---|---|---|
| I6 (repair out) | 314.5 s | 16.0 s to the crash | not reached |
| I5 (repair in) | 310.0 s | 60.4 s | 224.2 s |
| I7 (repair in, the fix) | 122.3 s | 34.8 s | 101.7 s |

The bodies the repair lets the checker reach cost about what the rest costs per declaration. Array3's
`asString` is the component's costliest member.

**Rung C: +109 s before the fix, +65 s after it.**
- In the apis: FortressLibrary's overloading check takes 167.9 s with rung C out and 208.0 s with it in
  (+24 %).
- In the component's typeCheck: 528.4 s against 594.8 s.
- Rung C was not measured on the distance stage. Its +24 % on that api's check is of the order of the
  review's +22 % for the distance stage's FortressLibrary (batch 15's review, section 1): a lead, not a
  measurement.

**Neither explains the 953 s.** The interpreted walker does: with rung C and the repair both in, splitting
the walker takes the stage from 935 s to 339 s.

## 4. The fix

- **`ScalaAstGenerator.java:625-650`.**
  - `walk(node)` calls `walkCases0(node)`.
  - The class cases are emitted in their old order, 30 to a method.
  - Each method but the last ends with `case _ => walkCases<k+1>(node)`.
  - The last ends with the old List, Option and default cases.
- **`FortressAst.scala`.** The generator's output, regenerated by `ant compileAll`.
  - The unedited generator reproduces the tracked file byte for byte.
  - The edited one writes the patched file.
  - Every other generated file is identical once ASTGen's timestamp line is masked, as the build masks it.
- **Method sizes after the fix** (bytes): `walkCases0` 2,215; `walkCases1` 3,373; `walkCases2` 4,099;
  `walkCases3` 4,072; `walkCases4` 4,186; `walkCases5` 4,378; `walkCases6` 4,474; `walkCases7` under 1,000.
- **Size of the patch:** 40 lines changed in the generator and 37 lines inserted in the generated file. The
  test file is new.
- **No switch.**

## 5. Why every answer stays (item 4)

The fix reads no rule differently, so the specification and the papers are not concerned.

A Scala `match` tries its cases in order and takes the first that matches. The split keeps every case, its
pattern and its body text unchanged, and in the same order.
- A value that matches none of a method's cases goes to the next method's first case. That case is the one
  that followed in the old single match.
- The last method keeps the old List, Option and default cases, in their order.
- So for every value the same case is chosen and the same code runs.
- The case bodies call `walk`, which a subclass may override, exactly as before. `walk`'s signature is
  unchanged.

The patch only inserts method boundaries between unchanged case lines. The audit (§7) checked this on every
branch of a full run.

## 6. Measurements

**Machine:** nproc=4; Intel(R) Xeon(R) Processor @ 2.10GHz, 2100.000 MHz; openjdk 25.0.4.1; `FORTRESS_THREADS=1`.
Nothing else of mine ran beside a timed run. A sampler recorded the load every minute, and the java process
count was 1 throughout. Two runs had brief light work of mine beside them: niced JFR reading during T1 and
scalac compiles during I5. Their highest 1-minute load was 1.79 and 1.95.

| run | start UTC | load at start | seconds | what |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| T1 | 19:48:54 | 0.91 | 953 | count stage, repair in (stock stage, limit raised) |
| T2 | 20:04:47 | 1.04 | 332 | plus a split testing `Node` first (variant C, not taken) |
| T3 | 20:10:19 | 1.22 | 344 | plus the split in order (first form of the patch) |
| I5 | 20:16:40 | 0.89 | 935 | instrumented, repair in |
| I4 | 20:32:15 | 1.04 | 826 | rung C out |
| I6 | 20:46:01 | 1.07 | 668 | repair out |
| I7 | 20:57:09 | 1.07 | 339 | the fix |
| I8 | 21:02:48 | 1.09 | 274 | the fix, rung C out |
| I9 | 21:07:22 | 1.03 | 652 | `-XX:-DontCompileHugeMethods`, no fix |
| D1 | 21:18:23 | 1.62 | 2,375 | distance stage, repair in (FortressLibrary 1,336, RangeInternals 762) |
| D2 | 21:58:01 | 1.03 | 931 | distance stage, repair and fix (FortressLibrary 462, RangeInternals 381) |
| F0 | 22:45:39 | 1.53 | 911 | final build, old walker first on the classpath, repair in a shadow |
| F1 | 23:00:50 | 1.02 | 352 | final build (the fix), repair in a shadow |

**Answers, run against run.**
- **The count stage's table:** T1, T2, T3, I5, I7, I9, F0 and F1 give
  `#total 39`, `#locations 38`, `#crash none`, every api 0. That equals the cited idle run of 2026-10-14
  (`diff` prints nothing).
- **The checker's whole output:** T1 = T2 = F0 = F1, after masking the tree's path.
- **The distance stage:** D1 and D2 tables are equal but for `#seconds` and `#machine`. `errors.tsv` is
  identical (49 errors), and so is the whole output.
- **The repair on the distance stage:** D1 equals climb batch 15's landed `distance.txt` but for its crash
  row. With the repair in, the crash row goes (`#crash none`) and no site comes.

## 7. The audit

The audit variant of the walker checks, at every branch it takes, the index of that branch against the index
the original single match takes. The original's index is recomputed by its own tests in its order: equality
for the 15 stable identifiers, then the class tests, then List, Option, default.

    @@AUDIT walk branches taken=279692861 mismatches=0 distinct-branches=90 of 216

The audited run's table reads 38 / 37: row 488's `:130` is missing. The counting copies hash AST nodes. That
changes the JVM's identity-hash sequence, and with it the api order (§9). The JFR run (prof1) lost `:130` the
same way. Neither run's walker is the patch's.

## 8. The tests

`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/nodes/WalkerJUTest.java` is in the misc track and has four
tests:

- `testEveryMethodCompilable`: every method of `Walker` is at most 8,000 bytes of bytecode, read with
  `java.lang.classfile`.
- `testIdentityWalkRebuildsNodes`: walked types are equal to the original and are new objects.
- `testOtherValuesComeBackAsTheyAre`: a String, a Span, an Integer, a `KindOp` node, None and Nil come back as
  the same objects.
- `testOverrideReachesNestedNodes`: an override reaches type variables nested in static arguments, tuples,
  arrows, intersections, unions, Options and Lists.

**The runs.**
- On the base build's classes (2026-10-14 22:15 UTC):

      java -cp <test classes>:<base build classpath> junit.textui.TestRunner com.sun.fortress.scala_src.nodes.WalkerJUTest
      .F...
      1) testEveryMethodCompilable(...)junit.framework.AssertionFailedError: Walker.walk is 31704 bytes of bytecode, more than 8000
      Tests run: 4,  Failures: 1,  Errors: 0

- With the fix built: `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=WalkerJUTest` gives "Tests run: 4, Failures: 0, Errors: 0",
  BUILD SUCCESSFUL.
- The test was written after the shadow prototypes, as a probe's is. Its failing run is on the base build.
- It is in Java because scalac 2.13 cannot read `java.lang.classfile`: "illegal cyclic reference involving
  class CodeImpl".

**The suites, with the fix built and without the repair:**
- `ant testQuick`:
  - compiler 1,212, library 86, othercompiler 263, all with 0 failures;
  - BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 4 min 34 s.
- `ant testFast`:
  - 1,988 tests, 0 failures, BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 5 min 0 s;
  - misc track: 427 tests, the landed gate's 423 plus these 4.
- `ant testSystem`:
  - 149 + 150 + 161 + 161 = 621 tests, 0 failures;
  - 2 min 16 s.

The counts equal climb batch 15's gate. The walker is shared by both paths' phases (the disambiguator, the
desugarers), hence `testSystem`.

## 9. Row 488: the checker's output depends on identity hashes

Every ASTGen node's `generateHashCode` starts from `getClass().hashCode()`, the `Class` object's identity
hash (for example `ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/nodes/TraitType.java:104`; 936 node classes do this).

So the order of every `HashMap` and `HashSet` of nodes depends on the JVM's identity-hash sequence. That
includes the apis that `StaticChecker.checkApis` iterates (`StaticChecker.java:125`). The sequence moves
whenever any code asks for an identity hash at a different moment.

**The runs.** The fixed checker ran with a copy of the stage's driver that first asks for N identity hashes
(`-Dprobe.hashes=N`):

| run | N | api check order | table | output |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| H0 | 0 | the usual one | 39 / 38 | identical to T1's |
| H1 | 1 | wholly different, starting RangeInternals, FortressLibrary, NativeArray | 39 / 38 | three messages print a union's members the other way |
| H2 | 1000 | another order | 39 / 38 | one message differs the same way |

The messages that changed in H1:
- `:1463`: `OR(O0,I0)` became `OR(I0,O0)`.
- `:3367`: `OR(T,IntLiteral)` became `OR(IntLiteral,T)`.
- `:3384`: `OR(T,IntLiteral)` became `OR(IntLiteral,T)`.

The two instrumented runs that hash nodes or add threads (JFR, the counts) lost `:130`.

This is a lead for row 488's "mechanism unknown". The fix asks for no identity hash, which is why its outputs
are identical.

## 10. What a landing would carry (item 5)

- **`fix.patch`, applied and built with `ant compileAll`.** The build regenerates `FortressAst.scala` from the
  generator and reproduces the patch's file, so the two stay in step.
- **`WalkerJUTest`.** Its failing and passing runs are in §8.
- **No switch.**
- **With row 680's line in the same tree**, the count stage takes 352 s idle (F1), with the table above: 39
  errors, 38 locations, no crash.
  - About 447 s with the 27 % allowance for load, inside the 690 s of `CLIMB-BATCH-15.md:154`.
  - The repair's own landing promotes `XXXLocalFunctionSiblingInLoop` and `XXXLocalFunctionSiblingCall` and
    re-keys the recursive case to 'reference cycle', as `e75bb538b` says.
- **The distance stage** with both: 931 s and 49 errors, the crash row gone.
- **The gate.** The fix touches a walker that both paths' phases use, so its suites are the whole gate.
  - My `testFast` and `testSystem` runs were on the fix alone.
  - The repair adds its three test changes.

## 11. Decisions, findings, questions

**Decisions.** No decision of the curator covers 1 to 6.

1. **The split in order (variant B).** Rejected:
   - variant C, which tests `Node` first and skips 213 tests for leaves: 332 s against B's 344 s, one run
     each, within noise; its exactness needs a proof (every node class implements `Node`);
   - the JVM switch alone: 652 s, and a switch every JVM would need;
   - a class-keyed dispatch.
2. **30 cases per method.** The largest method is 4,474 bytes, against the limit of 8,000.
3. **The patch changes the generator and the file it writes, not the file alone.** A build would otherwise
   regenerate the old walker the next time `Fortress.ast` or a generator changes.
4. **An audit by branch index, not by memo hits.** The fix adds no memo.
5. **The test is in Java**, because of the scalac 2.13 limit (§8).
6. **The brief's "distance stage is `tools/count-run/`" read as `tools/distance/run.sh`.** `count-run.sh`
   runs each interpreter test under walk.

**Findings.**
- The interpreted walker (§2.2).
- The shares of the repair (+267 s) and of rung C (+109 s before the fix, +65 s after) (§3).
- After the fix, about 95 % of the component's time is in the solver's re-normalization of meets (§2.3).
- The checker's output depends on identity hashes (§9).
- The repair removes the distance stage's crash row and adds no site (§6).
- The other methods over the limit are negligible after the fix (§2.2).

**Defects.**
- **The interpreted walker.** My change repairs it (way 1), pinned by `WalkerJUTest`. No ledger row holds it;
  the row to write:
  - claim: the generated `Walker.walk` (`FortressAst.scala`, from `ScalaAstGenerator.java`) is 31,704 bytes
    of bytecode, past HotSpot's 8,000-byte huge-method limit, so the JVM never compiles it, and every phase
    that walks a tree runs it in the interpreter;
  - status: NEGATIVE-VERIFIED, closed by the fix's commit;
  - class: implementation gap (generator, speed);
  - spec: silent;
  - reproducer: `WalkerJUTest.testEveryMethodCompilable`;
  - found by: this probe.
- **The identity-hash dependence.** A note for row 488, with the H runs' commands and outputs (§9).

**Sentences of the specification made false:** none.

**For FACTS.**
1. **The fact.** The generated AST walker's `walk` was one method over HotSpot's 8,000-byte limit, so it ran
   interpreted. With it split in order, the count stage with row 680's repair takes 352 s instead of 911 s,
   and the distance stage 931 s instead of 2,375 s, with identical output.
   - What it means: row 680's line can land under the 690 s rule.
   - Test: `WalkerJUTest.testEveryMethodCompilable`.
   - Detail: §2.2 and §6.
2. **The fact.** The checker's output depends on the JVM's identity-hash sequence, because AST hashes include
   the `Class` identity hash. One extra identity hash at start reorders the api checks and the members of
   unions in messages.
   - What it means: the stages' outputs can move with an unrelated edit (row 488).
   - Command: the driver with `-Dprobe.hashes=1`.
   - Detail: §9.
3. **The fact.** Rung C's normal form costs 12 % of the count stage before the fix, 19 % after.
   - Detail: §3.

**Questions for the curator (decisions not taken).**
- Q1: land the walker split as its own rung ahead of row 680's line, or in the same rung?
- Q2: pursue the solver's re-normalization of meets (§2.3), about 95 % of what remains?
  - Ways: a memo of normalized meets shared across analyzers; fewer reductions in `Formula.and`'s fold.
- Q3: make AST hashing independent of identity hashes (row 488)? That would change iteration orders, and so
  message text, once.

**Commands worked out.**
- **JFR, read without the text dump.** A single-file Java program over `jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingFile`
  aggregates `jdk.ExecutionSample` within an epoch window, by self, inclusive, callers or callees. A frame's
  `getType()` (Interpreted, JIT compiled, Inlined) shows which methods the JVM never compiled.
- **Methods over the limit:** a `java.lang.classfile` scan of `ProjectFortress/build` for `Code` attributes
  longer than 8,000 bytes.
- **The AST generators by hand, in scratch:**
  1. `javac -cp <scala jars>:ProjectFortress/build:ProjectFortress/third_party/astgen/astgen.jar -d <dir>/build ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/astgen/*.java`.
  2. Copy `Fortress.ast` into `<dir>/astgen`.
  3. From there, `java -cp <dir>/build:<scala jars>:ProjectFortress/build:astgen.jar edu.rice.cs.astgen.ASTGen Fortress.ast`. The `.ast` file's `customClassPath ../build` finds the generators.
- **A huge method's compile attempts:** `-XX:-DontCompileHugeMethods -XX:+PrintCompilation`.
- **Moving the identity-hash sequence:** a driver copy that calls `new Object().hashCode()` N times before
  the phases.

<!-- The skeptic's review of fix.patch (the generated walker split into eight methods, with WalkerJUTest), by reading the patch and the code on main at 558ae0a10, rebuilding it in a worktree of its own, and timing one run of the count stage with row 680's repair on an idle machine. -->

# Skeptic's review: the generated walker split in order

## Verdict

**Approved.** No fixes, so there is no `fix-2.patch`.

- By reading, the split cannot change a result.
- The build regenerates the patch's file byte for byte.
- The test fails on main and passes with the fix.
- One idle run of the count stage, with the fix and row 680's repair, took **333 s**. Its whole output is identical to the idle run without the fix (959 s).

## 1. The results stay the same, by reading

- **The generated file only gains lines.** `git diff --numstat` on `FortressAst.scala` gives 37 lines added and 1 removed. The removed line is `def walk(node:Any):Any = {`. The added lines are:
  - `walk` delegating to `walkCases0`, at patched 1590-1591;
  - seven boundaries of 5 lines each, at 1653-1657, 1718-1722, 1783-1787, 1848-1852, 1913-1917, 1978-1982 and 2043-2047. Each boundary is `case _ => walkCases<k+1>(node)`, then the closing of one method and the opening of the next.
- **Every case keeps its pattern, its body and its place.** A diff made only of insertions cannot move or change a line.
  - The sizes are 30 class cases in each of `walkCases0` to `walkCases6`, and 3 in `walkCases7`, which is 213.
  - `walkCases7` then keeps `List`, `Option` and `case _ => node`, in their old order.
- **The generator** (`ScalaAstGenerator.java`, patched 625-670) builds the same `cases` list in the same order as before: `cList` reversed, ignored and abstract classes skipped.
  - The chunk loop never emits an empty method. When the count is a multiple of 30, the last full method gets the closing cases. With zero cases, `walkCases0` gets them.
  - The only `case _` before the last method is each method's own last case, which hands the value on to the next method.
- **No guards.** None of the 216 cases has an `if`.
- **Scala reads the patterns the same way in every method.** Each method has the same scope as the old `walk`, inside the same trait: `S*` stable identifiers and extractors at package level, and lower-case binders.
- **The order among class cases cannot matter at all.** I checked this with reflection over the built classes:
  - No case's class is a supertype of another's (0 pairs).
  - None of the 213 is abstract, and all 213 implement `Node`.
  - So at most one class case matches any value.
  - The 15 stable-identifier cases (`case SKindOp =>`, `FortressAst.scala:807-812`) compare by the extractor object's default `equals`, so they match no node.
  - Only "class cases before List, Option and the default" is order-sensitive, and that is kept.
- **Subclasses.** About 45 Scala subclasses extend `Walker`, per the grep. Many override `walk` and call `super.walk`. `walk` keeps its name and signature, and the case bodies still call the virtual `walk`.
  - No source defines a `walkCases*` member: grep over the whole repository, `tmp/` aside.
  - Scala would refuse an override without `override` anyway.
  - No user of `Walker` exists outside `ProjectFortress/src`.
  - No code or test inspects `Walker` stack frames. `FileTests.java:873` looks only for `Driver.evalComponent`.
- **Stack.** The old `walk` had `max_locals` 1,079. The new methods have 82 to 180 each, 1,107 summed over the whole chain. So an interpreted walk of a List, Option or String needs about the old frame's room plus small forwarder frames, and earlier node classes need far less.

## 2. The build makes the patch's file

**Setup.** No base build existed, since the probe's at 473ab6a30 was gone. So I built one at main's head 558ae0a10: `ant compileAll`, the library order and the BooleanOps walk run, then `git status` clean. I seeded `/home/user/fortress-sk16` from it.

**What I did.**
1. Applied `fix.patch` with `git apply`, which was clean.
2. Saved the patched `FortressAst.scala`, then put main's version back, so that the build had to regenerate it.
3. Ran `ant compileAll`: BUILD SUCCESSFUL, 40 s.
   - It printed `Processing .../Fortress.ast`.
   - `makeAST` ran because the generator's source was newer than `Library/FortressAst.fsi` (`build.xml:644-646`).

**What I found.**
- The regenerated `FortressAst.scala` is byte-identical to the patch's (`cmp`).
- The tree's whole diff, with the test file added, equals `fix.patch` except for its `index` lines.
- No other generated file changed: not `nodes/`, not `Library/FortressAst.fs*`.
- The base build also ran `makeAST` with the unedited generator and stayed clean. So the old generator reproduces main's file.

## 3. The test

**Fails on main.** I compiled `WalkerJUTest` against the base build's classes. `junit.textui.TestRunner` gave "Tests run: 4, Failures: 1": `testEveryMethodCompilable` fails with "Walker.walk is 31704 bytes of bytecode, more than 8000".

**Passes with the fix.** `ant testOnly -DtestPattern=WalkerJUTest` gives "Tests run: 4, Failures: 0, Errors: 0", BUILD SUCCESSFUL.

**It runs in the misc track.** The track includes `**/*JUTest.class` (`build.xml:1200`). On a clean build:
- scalac runs first and parses the Java sources for their signatures (`build.xml:753-783`);
- javac then compiles the test against the built `Walker` (`build.xml:785` onward).

**What it catches.**
- A later `Fortress.ast` change makes the build regenerate the walker. The size test reads the built `Walker.class` and fails on any method of `Walker` over 8,000 bytes, naming the method and its size.
- The margin is wide. The largest method is 4,474 bytes (about 149 bytes per case). A 30-case chunk would need about 267 bytes per case to pass the limit.
- It also catches a generator that goes back to one method.
- The behaviour tests catch a broken chain anywhere in `walkCases0` to `walkCases6`. List and Option sit in the last method, so with a broken chain `testOverrideReachesNestedNodes` would get them back unwalked.

**What it misses.**
1. Methods over the limit outside `Walker` (section 5).
2. A JIT bail-out on a method under the limit. Size is necessary for compilation, not sufficient.
3. A single dropped case of a node class that the tests do not sample. Only a handful of type nodes and `TypeArg` are walked.
4. Speculation churn. I ran `-XX:+PrintCompilation` for 150 s on the same stage:
   - All eight methods compiled at tiers 2, 3 and 4, with no `COMPILE SKIPPED`.
   - There were 80 "made not entrant: uncommon trap" recompiles. The last of them came at 88 s.

It guards the right thing for this defect.

## 4. The time and the results, measured once

**Tree.** The fix plus row 680's line (`Decls.scala:414`, `makeTryChecker(this)` to `makeTryChecker(newChecker)`), built with `ant compileAll`: 26 s, scalac recompiled everything.

**Stage.** A copy of `run.sh` in my `tmp/`, whose only change is `timeout -k 10 900` to `3000`.

**Machine.**
- nproc 4, Xeon at 2.10 GHz.
- Before the start: no java process. I waited until the 1-minute load was under 1.0.
- During the run: only the stage's java process and its `timeout` wrapper.
- Load sampled each minute: 0.98 at the start, then 1.14, 1.31, 1.11, 1.04, 1.05, and 1.02 at the end.

**Run.** 23:29:57 to 23:35:30 UTC: **333 s**, the whole `run.sh`, its javac included.

| run | seconds |
|---|---|
| this run (fix and repair) | 333 |
| probe's F1 (fix and repair) | 352 |
| probe's F0 (repair, no fix) | 911 |
| idle measure without the fix, at 994dc944c | 959 |

994dc944c has the same code as 558ae0a10: `git diff` of `ProjectFortress`, `Library`, `build.xml`, `bin` and the stage is empty. This run is well inside the 690 s rule of `CLIMB-BATCH-15.md:154`.

**Results.**
- The table equals `measure-680-run1-table.txt`: `#total 39`, `#locations 38`, `#crash none`, every api 0, `#shadow` matching.
- The whole checker output, 178 lines, equals `measure-680-run1-full-output.txt` once `/home/user/fortress-m680` and `/home/user/fortress-sk16` are masked. That includes the last line `### rc=-1`. The output holds no time lines.
- So under P-148 the checker accepts and refuses the same programs, with the same errors at the same places.

## 5. What else the landing must carry

**Must carry:**
- `fix.patch` as it stands. It applies cleanly to 558ae0a10.
- Row 680's line, with its own test changes (`e75bb538b`).
- The gate's suites, both of them: the walker is used by phases of both paths.
- The ledger row and the FACTS entries that the probe proposes (`REPORT.md` §11).

**Other generated walkers.** No method generated from `Fortress.ast` is near the limit after the fix. I scanned `ProjectFortress/build` with `java.lang.classfile` for methods of 5,000 bytes or more. The in-repo generators' Java visitors have one small method per class.

**Methods over or near the limit.** None needs to be in this landing. The probe measured them at 9 of 14,819 samples after the fix. They are candidates for a later pass:
- `NodeReader.readNode`, 14,026 bytes: a chain of 938 string comparisons that ASTGen's own serializer generates (`astgen.jar`, `generateSerializers yes`). It runs on every AST cache read (`ASTIO.java:150`).
- `Misc.checkExprMisc`, 12,893.
- `HygienicRenamer.walk`, 11,599.
- `ExprDisambiguator.walk`, 8,518: 6.5 % over, and both paths' disambiguation runs it.
- The Rats! parsers' `pCharLiteralContent$1`, 23,717, three copies.
- The parsers' `pidrest`, 7,617, four copies: 95 % of the limit.

## Fixes

None.

## For the curator

1. **Land it.** The stage with both the fix and the repair took 352 s (F1) and 333 s (this run), against 959 s without the fix, with identical output.
2. **Q1 of the report** (with the repair or ahead of it) is still yours. Nothing here prefers one or the other: the split changes no result either way.
3. **A wider guard is a decision not taken.** One test could scan the whole build for methods over 8,000 bytes, with an allow-list of today's six. It would catch the hand-written ones and any new one. It is not needed for this landing.
4. **A nit, not fixed.** The generator joins each case's two lines with a literal `"\n"` inside a `println` (patched `ScalaAstGenerator.java:646-647`, `:654`). The output is identical on Linux. Only a Windows build would mix line endings.
5. **Scratch.** The outputs of this review are in `/tmp/claude-0/-home-user-fortress/fe616d40-a9c6-56d7-9da1-7168a172765d/scratchpad/sk16/`:
   - `skeptic-run-full-output.txt`, `skeptic-run-table.txt`, `skeptic-run-log.txt` and `skeptic-run-load.txt`;
   - `skeptic-printcompilation-walker.txt`;
   - `sizes-base.txt`;
   - the checking programs `MethodSizes.java` and `SubCheck.java`.

   Both worktrees (`/home/user/fortress-skb`, `/home/user/fortress-sk16`) are removed. Nothing is committed or pushed.

def reason_problems(rid):
    out = []
    for k, r in REASONS[rid]:
        if not r or not r.strip():
            out.append((k, 'no reason'))
        elif '\n' in r or '`' in r or any(ord(c) > 127 for c in r):
            out.append((k, 'a reason is one ASCII line with no backtick'))
        elif not r.endswith('.') or len(r) > 240:
            out.append((k, 'a reason ends with a full stop and is at most 240 characters'))
    return out


if __name__ == '__main__':
    import subprocess, re, sys, os
    root = os.environ.get('FORTRESS_HOME', os.path.abspath(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__)), '../../../..')))
    bad = 0
    for rid, (b, c) in LISTS.items():
        rp = reason_problems(rid)
        print(rid, 'reasons', len(REASONS[rid]), 'for', len(b), 'briefing keys |', 'problems', len(rp))
        for k, why in rp: print('   PROBLEM', why, ':', k[:200])

        for name, keys in (('briefing', b), ('checks', c)):

            badk = [k for k in keys if not k.strip() or k.startswith('-') or re.search(r'["`$\\\n]', k)]
            if badk:
                print('   PROBLEM keys the script refuses', rid, name, badk); bad += 1
            if name == 'checks':

            r = subprocess.run(['bash', 'explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh', '--check'] + keys, capture_output=True, text=True, cwd=root)

            probs = [l for l in lines if 'not one' in l or 'NOT FOUND' in l or 'no match' in l.lower() or 'no line of' in l or 'no such file' in l]
            total = [l for l in lines if l.startswith('Total')]
            print(rid, name, 'keys', len(keys), 'exit', r.returncode, '|', total[0] if total else r.stderr.strip()[:200])

# workflow (explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js; explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/
# batch-redesign.md) from the record and the briefings of lists15.py, into $OUT15/manifest15.js ($FORTRESS_HOME/tmp
# by default, which is ignored); check15.js checks it and splices it. On batch 14's pattern (plan-14/manifest/

# for word as the rung's section, which every role on the rung reads (the worker, the skeptic, a judge and a repair
# round), its code-span backticks dropped and any ellipsis character written as three full stops, since the

# and the intro every agent reads from its "What every agent of the run reads first". No value is set at launch: the

HERE = os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))
sys.path.insert(0, HERE)
from lists15 import LISTS, REASONS, IDS

os.makedirs(os.path.dirname(OUT), exist_ok=True)

def ascii_text(t):
    t = t.replace('`', '').replace('…', '...')
    bad = [c for c in t if ord(c) > 127]
    assert not bad, ('non-ASCII left', bad, t[:120])
    return t


def between(text, start, end):
    i = text.index(start)
    j = text.index(end, i + len(start))
    return text[i + len(start):j]


# Section 3: one block per rung, from its heading to the next ### heading.
s3 = between(rec, '\n## 3. The rungs\n', '\n## 4. ')
heads = list(re.finditer(r'^### ([A-Z])\. (.*)$', s3, flags=re.M))
assert [h.group(1) for h in heads] == list(IDS), [h.group(1) for h in heads]
sections, titles = {}, {}
for i, h in enumerate(heads):
    rid = h.group(1)

    sections[rid] = ascii_text(body)
    titles[rid] = ascii_text(h.group(2))

mrung = between(s5, '\n### The manifest, rung by rung\n', '\n### What every agent of the run reads first\n')

A('// body(i), C\'s at body(i); no rung declares landsOnlyWith or a crash).')
A('// No value is set at launch. The base and the base build are args.base and')
A('// args.baseBuild. At most two agents run at once on this box, FIFO (FACTS.md, "The')
A('// Workflow harness runs two agents at once on this box"); the scatter starts the')
A('// longest expected worker first.')
A('// ===========================================================================')
A('')
A("const BATCH = '15'")
A("const BATCH_RECORD = 'explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-15.md'")
A("const BRIEFING_LISTS = 'explorations/compile-ladder/plan-15/manifest/lists15.py'")
A('')
for rid in IDS:
    A('const %s_SECTION = [' % rid)
    for l in sections[rid].split('\n'):
        A(js(l) + ',')
    A("].join('\\n')")
    A('')
for rid in IDS:
    f = FIELDS[rid]
    b, c = LISTS[rid]
    slug = f['slug']
    assert re.fullmatch(r'[a-z0-9-]+', slug), slug
    path = f['worktree']
    assert re.fullmatch(r'/home/user/fortress-[a-z0-9-]+', path), path
    joins = [] if f['joins the gate'] == 'none' else [x.strip() for x in f['joins the gate'].split(',')]
    A("const %s_ENTRY = { id: '%s', slug: '%s', path: '%s', branch: 'wip/%s', expectedMinutes: %d," % (rid, rid, slug, path, slug, int(f['expected minutes'])))
    cc = f['checker count']
    assert cc == 'none' or re.fullmatch(r'[0-9]+', cc), (rid, cc)
    A('    writesState: %s, testIsStage: %s, gateJoins: %s, expectedMoves: [],%s' % ('true' if yes(f['writes state']) else 'false', 'true' if yes(f['its test is the stage']) else 'false', js(joins), '' if cc == 'none' else ' expectedCheckerCount: %d,' % int(cc)))
    A('    title: ' + js(titles[rid]) + ',')
    A('    blurb: ' + js(f['blurb']) + ',')
    A('    section: %s_SECTION,' % rid)

content.content:
## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'F-87'` prints one entry by its number, and `$T 'P-48'` one of POSITIONS. `$T 'F-87+'` adds each entry that F-87 cites by its number, and each entry that cites F-87. `$T 'history:F-87'` prints its history. Run one when your brief or a note cites an entry by its number.
- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Write FACTS and POSITIONS only with `explorations/coordinator/tools/record.py`, never by hand. `add` gives a new entry its number, and `set` rewrites an entry. The tool writes the entry to `FACTS.md` or `POSITIONS.md`, and its earlier text to the history file beside it. It commits nothing: commit both files in one commit. Its header gives its usage.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, add each fact as a new entry in the section of its topic, in the commit that establishes it. Put its detail in a section of your report: the file:line citations, the commands with their output, and the measured numbers. Point the entry to that section, by your report's file and the section's heading. If your report is only your final message, hand the fact over instead. Spend no effort on the entry's wording: it is rewritten to the record's form after your work.
- If your brief does not let you write FACTS, hand each fact over in the "For FACTS" item of your report, with:
  - the fact as it stands now, in one sentence;
  - what it means for the work;
  - the number that a decision rests on, if any, with what it counts; if its parts belong to different ledger rows, the part of each row;
  - the test that fails if the fact stops holding, or the command and the output that show it;
  - the section of your report that holds the detail.
- If your brief lets you write FACTS, rewrite a wrong entry in place. Otherwise say in your hand-over that the entry is wrong, with the evidence.
- POSITIONS holds each of the curator's decisions, in one place. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.

content.content:
## Gather

The gather composes one local commit per approved rung on `main`; nothing is merged.

- **The order.** Ascending order of each rung's lowest edited line in the files two or more rungs share, so that a later hunk does not shift lines a landed record cites. Any `file:line` a record cites that an earlier hunk shifted is re-anchored by symbol. Tests cite the specification by section, never by line, so no test is re-anchored.
- **Each rung.** Its net diff is applied with `git apply --3way --index`. A conflict in unrelated regions is resolved by hand; one in the same logic is returned, not guessed. Its files are written from the journal where the branch lacks them, by the commands the brief renders per rung. For a repaired rung, `REPORT.md` and `record.md` are always rewritten from the repair round's texts.
- **The record folded.** The FACTS entry under its area. Ledger notes through `ledger.py note`. New rows through `ledger.py add FILE --section TITLE`, each `NEW-<rung>-<n>` placeholder replaced with its number everywhere the rung's files and tests cite it, before the rung's commit. The handover line, in the batch's `RECORD.md`, "Handover lines" (the old handover file is retired into PLAN's first section, which the coordinator keeps). The rung's "Revival change" section is folded into no file: both its parts are copied, word for word, into the batch's `RECORD.md` (below), and nothing is written under `.claude/`. Through batch 13 the gather folded each entry into the skill's `revival-changes.md` as the rung wrote it, and the cold reader that followed made a question's handle findable instead of deleting it: that is how the coordinator's agenda reached the skill (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, "How it got there").
- **Corrections still owed.** The skeptic's `leftForGather` items. Each sentence of the specification a rung lists as made false and did not edit, corrected to what the code does, each clause checked against its code line. Batch 8's gather saw rung Q's Appendix I Effect false and let it stand, and in batch 9 no stage saw the one rung K made false. Each took a review judge and a repair, 0.53M and 0.39M (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, section 5; `reviews/batch-9-review.md`, section 6).
- **Text mismatches.** A text mismatch the decisions do not settle is filed, not blocking ("Rules weighed by what they cost against what they protect", item 4).
- **Items for the curator.** The gather puts every item a rung, skeptic or judge returned into `PLAN.md`, under "Pavol's answers, in the order they are needed" when work waits on it, else under "Off the path, parked".
- **After the rungs.** One commit closes each row a landed rung fixed (`ledger.py close N --commit HASH --test NAME`, then `ledger.py check`). One commit writes the batch's `RECORD.md`, once, last: the order and why, each rung's commit, the rows opened and closed, each skeptic's fixes and the contested rulings by commit, the rungs that did not land, the points to report, where each item for the curator went, and last, under "Revival changes, for the skill writer", each landed rung's "Revival change" section, both parts word for word.

A rung that did not land has its `REPORT.md` and `SKEPTIC.md` taken out of its branch path by path, its findings folded under "Not landed", and its new rows added. None of its source is applied.

Files are staged by an explicit list and `git diff --cached --stat` is read before each commit. A commit touching a path outside `explorations/` and `.claude/` carries a `historical:` line.

## Review beside the gate

The review and the gate start together on the gather's commits. The review reads and never builds; the gate builds and never reads the record; the gate commits nothing, so the two never commit at once. Run side by side they took 14.7 minutes per batch off the serial tail. The review stays, once (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs"). Its six checks:

1. Overlaps between rungs, and what their changes do together.
2. Each skeptic's fix and each repair commit, as applied: it does what its finding says, its test seen failing on the worker's head and then passing in its maker's transcript, a settled fix's citation, a reverted fix gone.
3. The folded record: FACTS lines, `ledger.py check`, no `NEW-` placeholder left where a row is cited, every closed row fixed, the handover, the revival-change material in `RECORD.md` true of the landed code.
4. Each specification sentence a rung listed as made false, corrected.
5. The points to report, with `holdsPush`.
6. The items for the curator, in `PLAN.md`.

What it does with a finding:

- A record-only or mechanical defect it fixes itself, inside `explorations/`, in one commit.
- A finding settled by tests and records only it routes to the next batch, as `review-routed.N` in `PLAN.md`, with no judge.
- A finding whose repair touches source, library, checker, interpreter or specification goes to a judge, who rules `land`, `repair`, `drop` or `stop`. `land` is for a ruling settled by tests and records after all: its steps go to the next batch and no repair runs.

The review returns its heads before and after its corrections and every path outside `explorations/` they changed. A path the gate reads makes the gate beside it stale, and the gate runs again. Any other path is recorded beside the gate's summary.

A review that returns nothing after three attempts holds nothing: the batch lands on its gate, and `review-missing.1` is listed.

### A review that still blocks after its repair

There is one judge and one repair for the review, and no second review. When the review's repair returns nothing, stops or does not land, the code findings the judge upheld are listed as `review-unrepaired.N` for the next batch. They do not hold the push (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs"). A step that cannot be undone that the repair reports holds it, as a rung's does.

### A repair of tests and records only

After a repair on the merged tree, the review's or the gate's, the whole gate runs again only when the repair, or the review's corrections, changed a path the gate reads that is not a test file: under `ProjectFortress/` or `Library/`, or `build.xml` (the `coordinator` skill's `references/batch.md`, "Reserved points and repairs", and `fortress-repo`'s `references/gate.md`, "When to run it"). In batch 8 the gate ran a second time after a repair of one sentence of Appendix I, 24 minutes on the critical path, with tables identical but for timing (`reviews/batch-8-review.md`, section 4).

A test file is a `.fss`, `.fsi` or `.test` directly in `ProjectFortress/tests/` or a `ProjectFortress/*_tests/` directory.

- The repair returns its heads and changed paths. In `testRuns` it lists each test file it added or changed, run in the harness on the merged tree: the files of one corpus together in one JVM (`ONE_JVM=1 junit.sh`, and one `harness-one.sh` call for the interpreter tests).
- The gate runs again on a code path, a changed test no passing run exercises, a run that failed, or a repair that listed nothing.
- After the gate's repair it also runs again unless every red line is answered by a passing run (`failingAnswered`) and no suite count fell.
- When a red gate stood beside the review, and the review's repair of tests only answers its lines, no gate judge or gate repair runs.
- When the first gate's tables stand, the commit stage appends the runs to `summary.txt` as `# repair-tests` lines, and the paths no stage reads as `# repair-ungated` lines. `gate_compare` skips `#` lines.

`repairRerun` in the script decides.

## Gate

One run on the merged tree, its logs under `tmp/gate-batch-<N>/`, its three outputs written by fixed functions, never by hand. The functions of steps 5 and 7 (`gate_summary`, `gate_compare`, `last_landed_summary`, `ladder_filter`, `ladder_compare`, `mg_phases`) are in `tools/gate-functions.sh`, which the gate sources from the tree's root with `FORTRESS_HOME` set; until 2026-10-10 they were strings of the script (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, finding GA2). Its steps:

1. The disk.
2. `rm -rf ProjectFortress/TEST-RESULTS`, then `ant compileAll`, and at once the distance stage started in the background.
3. The library order if the build started the caches again, then two copies of the caches for the ladder.
4. `ant testFast`, then `ant testSystem`, never both at once, at four threads, pinned in `build.xml` (P-125, "The suites run Fortress in parallel."). Then `ant testSpecData` once an approved rung brings it into the gate, or the last landed summary has a `specdata/` row; every example must pass (P-124, "The specification's examples join the gate at zero red.").
5. `summary.txt` from `gate_summary`, one row per suite read from the plain-formatter files under `TEST-RESULTS/`, because the parallel tracks interleave their lines in the ant log. It ends with the `BUILD` and `Total time` lines and the machine it ran on (`# machine `, from `rung-flat-tower/machine.sh`), so that timings are read against their machine. `gate_compare` against the newest landed summary: a failure, an empty suite, a count that fell or a suite gone is red. The `system-<i>` shards are compared by their sum, since `testSystem` is one suite sharded by sorted index and a new file moves every later file along the shards; climb batch 2's gate went red on exactly that (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-2/JUDGE-gate.md`).
6. The four-thread atomic runs: 14 programs, three runs each, 42 lines. A FAIL, NO-PASS or compile failure is red; a timeout is re-run once.
7. The ladder regression (the skill's `gate.md`): the 85 files of the baseline's pass list compared on phase and output, the `Operation took` line masked, and the eighteen microGPT components compiled only. A DOWN, STDOUT or MISSING line is red unless a rung declared it.
8. The checker count, and 9. the distance, below.

A red gate goes to a judge, then one repair, then one more gate. A gate red after its repair stops the batch, nothing pushed.

### The checker count, and a rung whose test is that stage

The gate's step 8 runs the compiler's checker over the interpreter's library (`tools/checker-count/run.sh`, about 5 minutes since climb batch 13b: 387 s in 13b's gate, 303 s on batch 14's rung L's tree and under 5 minutes in its gate, against the stage's 900 s limit) and compares its total with the last landed one. That can run past the Bash tool's 300 s limit, so a rung's worker starts the stage detached with nohup and waits for it with `wait_for`, as the skill's `session.md`, "Long commands", gives them; the distance stage below runs the same way, about half an hour (26 to 29 minutes in batch 14). It answers the library route: one library, the interpreter's, becomes the library the compiler checks (P-37, "The library route."). The total is reported and never red (P-39, "The checker count is measured, never red."). A fix can raise it, because the checker stops checking an api at its first errors, and two rungs' changes do not add. `checker_compare` is red only on a crash line no rung declared, a stale shadow (the instrumented copy no longer matching the tracked checker), or a table with no total. The overloading checker's memo is off in the stage, since it hides 27 to 35 errors depending on build order.

A `testIsStage` rung has that stage as its test: its before is the last landed table, run once after the edit and rebuild. No program can yet be compiled against the interpreter's library, so this is the one place a permanent stage stands in for a test file.

A rung whose every path lies under `explorations/`, `Specification/`, `Documentation/`, a test corpus, the test harness's sources, or walk's evaluator and natives runs neither stage. Both stages run only the compiler's phases (F-111, "The checker-count and distance stages read only the compiler's phases ..."; `STAGE_BLIND`).

### The distance stage

The full measurement of the distance to the switch-over, reported and never red (P-39, "The checker count is measured, never red."). `tools/distance/run.sh` runs every stage of the checker over the twelve prelude components in one JVM, under shadows made from the tracked sources at each run, with the compiled path's setting and the implicit bound `Any`. An edit that no longer matches stops the run, and `#shadow` says STALE. It starts beside the suites right after `compileAll` and is read last; `compare.sh` prints DISTANCE DOWN, UP or SAME and what moved, and always exits 0. The commit stage lands `distance.txt` and the per-site list, `explorations/compile-ladder/gate/distance-sites.tsv`, which the next batch's rungs read as their before.

## No skill text

The batch writes no skill text. Each rung's "Revival change" material goes into the batch's `RECORD.md`, under "Revival changes, for the skill writer". After the landing, the standing skill writer writes the skill from it, and a cold read of the changed parts follows ("After the landing: the coordinator's routing", step 4). One writer does the writing (the `coordinator` skill's `references/skill-rewrite.md`, "The method").

Through batch 13 the gather folded each rung's entry into the skill's `revival-changes.md`, the review could correct it there, and a cold reader read it beside the gate's tail and made a handle findable instead of deleting it. That carried question handles, decision status and batch records into a part that workers load (`reviews/skills-agenda-audit.md`, "How it got there"). The batch's cold reader and its `coldread.N` and `delta-unfolded.N` items are gone with the fold.

The commit stage checks that nothing under `.claude/` changed since the base (step 2, below).

## Commit, and the push held

The commit stage:

0. Starts the quick microGPT walk check in the background, unless an earlier attempt started it (`tools/mg-run.sh`, the quick pair, about a minute; P-30, "The microGPT walk check is quick."). It waits for the result before it returns. Unless both programs print `ALL PASS`, `microgpt-walk.1` is listed. It holds nothing.
1. Copies the gate's outputs into `compile-ladder/climb-batch-<N>/gate/` and the per-site list into place. It writes the landed figures into FACTS, numbers only: "The true distance to the switch-over" and "The checker-count stage's table". It builds the specification's PDF once if a landed commit changed `Specification/`.
   1a. Appends the repair runs and the paths no stage reads beside the summary, where the first gate's tables stand.
2. Checks every commit since the base: the skill's footer, no model identifier, and a `historical:` line where a commit touches the 2012 tree. Then it runs `git diff --name-only <base> HEAD -- .claude/`, which should print nothing. Each path it prints is listed as `skill-touched.N`, for the coordinator; it holds nothing.
3. Pushes `main` to `origin` and to `claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8` and `blinded-fable`, retrying a failed push up to four times (the protocol's hard rules).
4. Removes each rung's worktree without `--force`, with its ignored `tmp/` and the old code's caches folder. It keeps one git refuses, and names it, since it holds uncommitted work.

The push is held when any landed rung's worker or skeptic, the review, or a merged-tree repair reports a point with `holdsPush` true, or a malformed one: a step that cannot be undone or acts against a decision on record. The stage then pushes nothing, keeps the worktrees, and writes a "Not pushed." paragraph into `RECORD.md`; the coordinator pushes once the curator lifts it. Batch 5's push went out past an unlifted stop because nothing held it (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-5/RECORD.md`). A rung that did not land holds nothing.

The curator's rule on gate reruns ends: "The same weighing of cost against what a rule protects applies to the other rules of the batch workflow." The rules in force from that weighing (batch N's review, `reviews/batch-N-review.md`, question 4):

# Running and reviewing a batch

The batch workflow is `explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.js` and its manual, `climb-batch-workflow.md` beside it. Its stages run in this order: the scatter of the rungs, the rung workers, the skeptics, the judges and the repair round, the gather, the merged-diff review, the gate, and the commit stage. Read a stage's section of the manual when you reach it: `facts-extract.sh 'doc:explorations/coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md#<heading>'`.

**batch record**
: `explorations/coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-<name>.md`, written by the planner before the launch. Its rung sections are the workers' briefs; its other sections are for the curator.

**base**
: Commit that the batch starts from.

**gather**
: Stage that merges the rungs and folds their reports and record lines into the tree.

**merged-diff review**
: Review of the gathered diff, beside the gate, of the records, the reserved points and the routing.

**repair round**
: One round of fixes after the merged-diff review or the gate.

**commit stage**
: Last stage, which commits the landed tree and runs the pass of `references/record.md`.

**reserved point**
: Point that a batch record keeps for the curator, such as a model or APL line beyond the approved ones, or an interpreter output that a rung cannot explain.

**checker count**
: Errors that the compiled checker reports on the interpreter's library, up to each component's first error.

**distance**
: All the checker's errors on that library, which must reach zero before the switch-over: the move of the compiled path onto the interpreter's library.

## The go

- The batches of PLAN's phase 3 run on a standing go, in PLAN's order. Launch each when the batch before it has landed and its own batch record has no open question.
- If a question that the batch record raises is consequential (`SKILL.md`), put it to the curator first. Otherwise decide it and put it on the review list. While the curator is away, overnight, take its recommended default and put it on the review list. If that default would reverse a decision of the curator, hold that batch, and launch the repair batch (`explorations/coordinator/REPAIR-BATCH.md`) in its place.
- Have one Fable review read each coming batch record before the launch, with a go in advance. It is written for the curator in place of reading the record. Treat its questions as the batch record's.

## The workflow

- Between batches, improve the script and the manual where a batch showed a problem.
- Let every step spend the fewest workers that it needs.
- Build the base once, yourself, in a worktree where nobody compiles or runs (`args.baseBuild`). Every rung worktree is seeded from it (`explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh`), never built clean.
- No stage runs a build, a suite or a measurement again on a code state that another stage ran, and no agent reads again a log that has not changed.
- Let the planner give each rung its mission briefing, from the territory map (`explorations/coordinator/map/`), in neutral words: "the decisions on record", not the curator's name. Require no answers from the worker about how it searched.
- At each landing, report the share of agents that read the briefing in their first turn. Aim for about 80 percent, the share it once had; it fell to 25 to 35.

## The roles

- The skeptic checks a rung's result after its worker, and builds nothing to check. It reads from the worker's transcript whether the test came first and failed. It runs its own small programs on the rung's build, and on the base through `explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh` with a private caches folder. Where the rung changes the compiled checker, the skeptic also runs the count stage itself, on the base build and on the worker's commits, as `fortress-repo`'s `compiler.md`, "The checker's time", gives a reviewer. That run is the one exception to this bullet and to the rule that no stage measures a code state again.
- It checks the result against the library's way, the ledger, sibling sites and the decisions on record, and fixes what it finds, test first.
- A judge rules only on a fix that the skeptic marks contested, on a rung that the skeptic refuses, or on a rung whose worker reported that it could not go on. The first ruling runs on Opus, a second on Fable (`judgeTier`). A settled fix lands with the review and the gate as its check. Reaching a reserved point, or a file outside what the rung's section of the batch record names, does not make a settled fix contested: it lands, and the point or the file goes on the review list. A point that cannot be undone holds the batch.
- No batch compares the printed outputs of the suites' test programs, and no baseline is run to compare against.

## The checker count and the distance

The gate reports the checker count in every batch, and the distance in phase 3. Neither turns the gate red.

- If a rung's test is the checker count or the distance, it takes the last landed gate's tables as its starting values.
- If every file that a rung changes lies outside what the two measures read, the rung runs neither and lists those files (`STAGE_BLIND`). Its skeptic checks the list against the branch's diff.
- The review after the batch ties every new or risen row of the count's table to a named rung edit.
- The gate's comparisons hide Java line numbers, identity hashes and moved library positions. Put every difference that they hid on the review list. Put there too each line of the team's tests that a rung rewrote to keep its checked value, with its before and after.

**The answers this rung follows.** Each row is gated by an expected failure and traced to its line (PLAN, its lines for rows 707 and 709, and "Climb batch 14, listed for his review"). usage: facts-extract.sh [--check] [--part N] [--page-bytes N] [--root DIR] [--common] [QUERY ...]

Prints what the queries name, whole and in the order they are given; a rung's
briefing is one such command. Each piece comes under a line naming its file
and section. The output comes in parts of at most PAGE_BYTES (default 28000);
part 1 opens with the size of the whole output in bytes and estimated tokens,
then what was asked for, where it is and what was not found; each part says
whether there is a next one, and --part N prints part N.

QUERY is one of:
  F-87, P-48             the entry of that number in FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md
  F-87+                  the entry, then each entry it points to and each entry
                         that points to it, each once, one level
  history:F-87           the entry's blocks in FACTS-history.md or
                         POSITIONS-history.md, oldest first: the provenance line
                         of each change and the line it replaced
  TITLE                  the FACTS.md entry whose title holds TITLE: an entry's
                         title is its bold opening, or where it has none, its
                         opening words up to the first colon, semicolon or full
                         stop; when no current title holds it, the entry one of
                         whose former titles (in FACTS-history.md) does, with a
                         line saying it was retitled
  section:HEADING        every entry of the FACTS.md section whose heading holds HEADING
  index:WORDS            the INDEX.md lines that hold every one of WORDS (at most 10)
  ledger:ROW             row ROW of the gap ledger, whole, under its section and
                         the table's header
  ledger-find:WORDS      one line for each gap ledger row that holds every one of
                         WORDS: its number, its status and the first 150 characters
                         of its claim (at most 10, then how many more matched)
  positions:TITLE        the entry of POSITIONS.md whose bold title holds TITLE, as
                         a TITLE query does in FACTS.md, former titles included;
                         exactly one must, else the nearest titles are named
  positions:DATE WORDS   the entry of POSITIONS.md dated DATE (YYYY-MM-DD, the first
                         date in the entry) whose head, the entry's text up to its
                         first colon and space, holds every one of WORDS; when no
                         entry of POSITIONS.md matches, the entry of
                         POSITIONS-history.md, from the latest of its sections
                         that hold one, with the line saying what became of
                         it; the output says which file it came from
  map:FILE#HEADING       the section of explorations/coordinator/map/FILE whose
                         heading holds HEADING, down to the next heading of its level
  doc:PATH#HEADING       the same for any note, PATH from the repository root, such
                         as a judge's ruling; doc:PATH alone prints the whole note;
                         in a .tex or .tick file the headings are its \chapter, \section,
                         \subsection, \subsubsection and \paragraph titles,
                         matched with their macros dropped; a heading equal to
                         HEADING wins over the headings that merely hold it, and
                         HEADING may be a path, A > B, for B's section inside A's
  map:FILE#HEADING@WORDS, doc:PATH#HEADING@WORDS
                         only the table rows and list items of that section that
                         hold every one of WORDS, a row under its table's header,
                         and the paragraphs whose bold lead holds them
  code:PATH#FROM         the declaration that starts on the one line of PATH that
                         holds FROM, with its line numbers: in .java, .scala and
                         .js through the brace that closes it, elsewhere (.fss,
                         .fsi) through its more indented lines and its end
  code:PATH#FROM..TO     from the declaration at FROM through the end of the
                         one at the first line after it that holds TO
WORDS match as whole words, or as the start of one when a word ends in *.
Matching ignores case, backticks and double quotes, reads curly quotes as

## 7. Decisions taken here, reported to Pavol

1. **What the per-provider check reads in a component.** Three readings were considered:
   - (a) Every declaration, abstract included, with the `implemented` filter. This is closest to the letter of "provides". It would also read a component's own abstract re-declarations of its api's traits, so each per-provider site in an api would appear a second time in the component that implements it. An object below such a trait must implement every abstract method it inherits, and its own declaration is then the meet, so these pairs carry no run-time ambiguity.
   - (b) Taken: bodies, plus every declaration whose declaring trait is not declared in the unit. This is the top-level set's own convention (`OverloadingChecker.scala:80-88`). It closes finding 1 and the older two-api hole, and adds no check of a component's own abstract pairs.
   - (c) Bodies only. This is finding 1.

   (b) is the narrowest reading that closes every run-time ambiguity the skeptic measured.
2. **How the self parameter is compared in the per-provider meet.** As the receiver is in the Meet Rule for Dotted Methods: by subtyping, which `oa.lteq(ha, fa)` and `oa.lteq(ha, ga)` already check on the full domains, with the meet of the other parameters compared without it. At self position 0 this computes exactly what the base computes (`TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:67-72`). The alternative, dropping from `allMethods` the declarations that `C`'s own declaration keeps it from inheriting (`traits.tex:520-527`), needs a transitive inheritance computation in `STypesUtil.scala`, rung I's file. It was not taken.

## 4. Finding B: the judge's decision 1 rests on a premise the compiled checkers do not hold (older; report correction and a row)

The decision is to leave a component's own abstract functional methods unread by the per-provider check (`OverloadingChecker.scala:139-141`). It was argued from "An object below such a trait must implement every abstract method it inherits, and its own declaration is then the meet, so these pairs carry no run-time ambiguity" (`JUDGE.md`, decision 1 (a)). The report repeats the argument: in section 5 (3), "for pairs an object must implement anyway, where its own declaration is the meet"; in section 11; and in `forPavol`'s first entry.

The object need not declare its own, and that is what `SkAbsConc` shows:
- `A` declares an abstract `pick(self)`, `B` a concrete one, and `object O extends { A, B } end` declares none;
- it compiles on the base, the pre-repair and the head, and every run prints `b`, `b`, the second for `x: A = O`;
- walk stops with an `InterpreterBug`, picking `A`'s abstract declaration (row 100's mechanism).

**What the specification says.** The program is invalid twice over:
- `O` inherits `A`'s abstract method and "any object inheriting an abstract method must define a body expression for the method" (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:571`);

# Climb batch 16

## 1. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. It runs a program without static types. The **compiled path** checks a program's types with the **checker**, then makes JVM bytecode.
- **The one library** is the interpreter's library (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`). At the **switch-over** the compiled path takes it over.
- **The distance** is the number of errors the checker reports on the one library. Each error has a **site** (a file and a line).
- **The count** is the checker's errors on the library's apis and its `FortressLibrary` component, read by the **count stage**, which also gives the checker's time. Since climb batch 15b nothing stops it, so the count is the component's own errors.
- A **row** is an entry of the gap ledger, cited by number. An **item** is a numbered question in PLAN's list "Pavol's answers" or the review queue.
- A **rung** is one fix, built by one worker in its own copy of the tree and checked by a second worker, the skeptic. A **batch** is a few rungs, merged and tested together by the **gate** and landed at once.
- **Test first.** Every fix starts with a test that shows the defect, seen failing before the edit and passing after. An **expected failure** is a test named `XXX...` that passes while the defect is there; when the fix lands it is **promoted** to a plain name.
- **P-148**, your rule of 14 October: a rung that changes the checker times the count stage before and after its change, then makes a second pass that makes the checker faster without changing what it accepts, refuses or says.
- An **identity hash** is a number the JVM gives an object the first time it is asked for one. It depends on what ran before, not on the object, so anything ordered by it can change order between two runs.
- A **memo** keeps an answer the checker computed, so that the same question asked again is answered at once.

### Where the distance stands

- After climb batch 15b the distance is 49 and the count 39 (`compile-ladder/climb-batch-15b/gate/distance.txt`, `checker-count.txt`; gate `3cf18a2b3`). The count stage took 325 s at that gate, beside other stages; idle, 333 s and 352 s (the probe's `SKEPTIC.md` section 4, `REPORT.md` section 6).
- The 49 by what each waits on (`reviews/batch-15-review.md` section 1; unchanged at 15b):
  - 21, the arrays: 14 bodies typed by their parent trait, 3 sizes tested in a branch, 2 export errors, row 678's `Col` and `Row` 2.
  - 12, your other open items: the integer power 6, item 38's `String` pairs 3, row 634's list half 1, item 46's fused arm 1, row 631's `embiggen` 1.
  - 12, the `where` clauses; 3, row 731 (row 425's corrected text); 1, row 488.
- **No site is free to fix.** Every one waits on your answer, a language feature not built, or a checker project. So this batch moves no site on purpose. It makes the checker faster, makes its output the same from run to run, and repairs rows outside the distance on both paths.
- What the batch does to the tables:
  - S: none by design; its test is that nothing changes.
  - H: none by reading, but the order of three messages may change once, and row 488's site at `:130` may go or stay. Either way it then stays put.
  - K: two sites move to the lines of the calls they are about (`:3405` to `:3422`, `:3411` to `:3424`), by reading; none comes or goes.
  - W: none; it edits walk only, which the stages do not read.
- **The distance expected after the batch: 49, or 48 if `:130` goes with H.** **The count: 39, or 38 likewise.** Both are reported, never red.

### The rungs, two sentences each

- **S, the checker's solver faster, and a guard on the build's long methods.** About 95 % of the checker's time over the library component is the solver normalizing the same meets again and again; S makes it reuse those answers, or reduce less often, by whichever way a profile shows a gain, and proves on one full run that every reused answer equals the one computed fresh. It also adds one test that fails when any method of the build grows past the length HotSpot compiles, with today's few on an allow-list.
- **H, the syntax tree's hashes apart from the JVM's identity hashes.** Every node's hash starts from a number the JVM picks for its class, so the checker's output can change order with an unrelated edit, and row 488's site comes and goes; H starts each hash from the class's name instead. Its test is that the checker's whole output is one and the same however the JVM's numbers fall.

### Q1. May the checker refuse an object that inherits an abstract method from one trait and its body from another (rows 572 and 727; review-queue item 62)?

**The question in plain words.** A functional method is declared with `self` among its parameters and called `pick(x)`. A trait may leave one abstract, with no body. Take:

```
trait A  pick(self): String  end           (* abstract *)
trait B  pick(self): String = "b"  end     (* a body *)
object O extends { A, B } end              (* declares no pick of its own *)
```

`pick(O)` has two candidates, `A`'s and `B`'s, and neither is more specific. The specification refuses `O` twice: an object must define each abstract method it inherits (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:571`), and a type that provides two such declarations must provide one on their meet (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Meet Rule"; "provides" includes abstract declarations, `traits.tex:528-529`). Today the compiled path accepts `O` and runs `B`'s body, also for a call typed by `A`; walk stops with an internal error (row 572). The cause is one filter: in a component the checker reads no abstract functional method of a trait the component declares (`OverloadingChecker.scala:138-141`), while it reads abstract dotted methods (`:183-193`), where it refuses the same shape written `o.m()`. The same filter lets a trait declare `f(self, y: S): ZZ32` abstract beside `f(self, y: S): ZZ32 = 2`, two identical declarations, and the code generator then crashes on them (row 727).

**Why it comes to you.** Climb batch 8's judge chose not to read those declarations (its decision 1, way (b)), and that default is on your review list as item 62, "default left with the row". Reading them, the judge's way (a), refuses both shapes. The sources split: the specification, the type group's rules (P-26) and the team's own dotted check refuse; Java refuses `O` too ("inherits abstract and default"); Scala accepts it, a concrete member implementing an abstract one from any trait. For row 727's single-trait shape all agree: Java and Scala refuse a method declared twice.

**The ways.** (a) The checker reads them, keeping today's rule that an abstract declaration implemented by a subtype's body with the same parameter types is not checked against it; rows 727 and 572 close, the code generator's crash becomes the checker's refusal. (b) Leave them unread, item 62's default; the rows stay. Item 62's other way, an abstract-method check that demands the object's own declaration, refuses row 572 only.

**Default: (a), and rung K builds it.** It is reversible: one condition of one filter. ```
trait A  pick(self): String  end           (* abstract *)
trait B  pick(self): String = "b"  end     (* a body *)
object O extends { A, B } end              (* declares no pick of its own *)
```
